1.0.0.en: Striking the Amalekites: fighting the Amalekites.

1.0.1.en: Ziklag: a city lying in the south of the land of the tribe of Judah, then given to the tribe of Simeon. Afterwards the Philistines took it, then Achish, king of the Philistines, returned it to the children of Israel. When David was away from it, the Amalekites attacked it and burned it, so David fought them, recovered it and took much spoil, and he stayed in it to restore it. The camp: the encampments of the soldiers of the children of Israel during the war.

1.0.2.en: The First Book of Samuel ended by mentioning two events: David's victory over the Amalekites and his recovery of the spoil and the captives, and the other event, the death of Saul and his sons in his war against the Philistines. The beginning of the Second Book completes for us the sequence of these events. It mentions that after David returned to Ziklag and stayed in it two days, on the third day a stranger came from the battlefield of the Philistines with Saul, his clothes torn and earth upon his head, a sign of great grief, whether it was real grief or feigned, to give those he met the impression that he was pained by the news he carried. This man came to David and bowed down before him to honor him, and perhaps he hoped to gain a position with David by announcing to him the death of his enemy Saul.

1.0.3.en: It is noticed that David did not send to learn the news of the war, lest anyone think that he wished for Saul's death and was eager to obtain the kingdom. Indeed, he was not eager for that.

1.1.0.en: David asked him where he had come from, and he told him that he had escaped from the camp of Israel to save his life.

1.2.0.en: David knew of the battle that had taken place between the children of Israel and the Philistines, the battle in which Achish's men had prevented him from taking part (see 1 Sam 29:4). So he asked him eagerly what had happened in the war, and the man answered him that the fighters of Israel had fled from the field because they could not stand firm before the armies of the Philistines, and many of them had fallen dead, and Saul and Jonathan his son had also died. The man meant to bring David the good news that King Saul and Jonathan the crown prince had died and that he himself had become king. We note that David knew that the Spirit of God had departed from Saul and that he was exposed to death in this war, yet he did not send messengers to learn the result of the war, lest anyone think that he was seeking Saul's death in order to reign in his place.

1.3.0.en: To make sure of the death of Saul and Jonathan, David asked the man how he knew that they had died, because he loved them and wished that the news were untrue and that what the man had heard were mere rumor.

1.4.0.en: "As I happened": by chance, that is, this man was not one of the soldiers fighting with the children of Israel, but was passing by chance on this mountain where the battle took place.

1.4.1.en: Mount Gilboa: the north-eastern part of Mount Ephraim, lying between the River Kishon and the valley of the Jordan. It rises about 500 meters above the sea and has narrow valleys within it.

1.4.2.en: The man made him understand that he learned of it by chance, as he was on Mount Gilboa where the battle between the two armies took place, and he saw Saul leaning on his spear and the Philistine warriors coming toward him to kill him. (Up to here the man's account agrees with what is in 1 Sam 31.)

1.5.0.en: From here on the man's testimony differs from what the inspired text relates in (1 Sam 31:4), for the man claims that Saul, as he was looking behind him, saw him and called him, and the man answered and came to him. The truth is that Saul spoke with his armor-bearer and not with this man; he is lying to show David that he killed his enemy Saul, so that he might receive a reward from him.

1.6.0.en: The man went on with his claims about what had happened, and mentioned that Saul asked him who he was, and he answered him that he was an Amalekite, and perhaps he had lived among the children of Israel and joined them.

1.7.0.en: The man claimed that Saul asked him to come near and thrust him through with the sword, because he felt dizzy, though he was still alive.

1.7.1.en: (This conversation had taken place between Saul and his armor-bearer, as is recorded in (1 Sam 31:4), but the Amalekite falsely claimed that Saul's words were addressed to him.)

1.8.0.en: "I stood upon him": I came near him after he had fallen to the ground.

1.8.1.en: The man continued in his lie, saying that he did come near to Saul and killed him, justifying it by saying that he saw Saul's severe wounds and that he would surely die. He took the crown that was on Saul's head and the gold bracelet that was on his arm and brought them to David, thinking that David would be pleased with the news of Saul's death and would reward the man for this good news. He did not invent a story showing that he had killed Jonathan, because he knew that David loved Jonathan and did not want to provoke David's anger over the killing of Jonathan.

1.8.2.en: Some think that Saul's armor-bearer was Doeg the Edomite, and that this Amalekite man was his son, because Amalek was descended from Edom, and that Doeg was the one who killed Saul, as is mentioned in (1 Sam 31:4), and he sent Saul's crown and bracelet with his son to David to bring him the news, and then killed himself out of grief for his master Saul.

1.9.0.en: The impact of the news upon David was very painful, contrary to what the Amalekite had expected. David and his men grieved, and all of them tore their clothes as a sign of great sorrow.

1.9.1.en: David did not gloat over Saul's death, although Saul had pursued him all his life. This is evidence of David's forgiveness, the purity of his heart and his love for his enemies.

1.10.0.en: The men mourned the dead with sorrowful words, and wept aloud and fasted until evening, seeking the mercies of the Lord for the souls of the dead. Their grief was great for Saul their king, for Jonathan the brave and faithful friend of David, and for the people of the Lord who had been killed in the war.

1.11.0.en: David asked the man who had come to him with this heartbreaking news where he was from, and the man answered him that he was the son of a stranger, an Amalekite.

1.12.0.en: David rebuked the man for his boldness in killing Saul, and asked how he was not afraid to stretch out his hand against the Lord's anointed, who had been anointed with the holy oil, when the Lord has warned against this, as in (Ps 105:15), "Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm."

1.13.1.en: "Thy blood be upon thy head": bear your guilt.

1.13.2.en: David commanded one of his young men to kill the Amalekite, and the young man did so. His killing was the recompense for his killing of Saul, as he confessed himself, when David told him that he bore the punishment for what he had done. This was the first case in which David judged as king after the death of Saul, and it shows his justice and his love for his enemies.

1.13.3.en: Do not rejoice at the misfortunes of those who wrong you, but have compassion on them, pray for them, make excuses for them in their wrongs against you, and look at their virtues so that you may love them. Then you will be able to stretch out a helping hand to them in their afflictions.

1.14.0.en: This lament was an eloquent literary work to mourn Saul and Jonathan his son. David did not gloat over Saul's death, but grieved greatly over his death.

1.15.0.en: Bow: a flexible metal rod with a string of leather tied between its two ends, so that it bends into the shape of an arc. The arrow is placed between the string and the bow, the bow is pushed forward and the string drawn back, and the arrow is aimed at the target; then the string is released and the arrow flies to its mark.

1.15.2.en: Jasher: its meaning is upright or righteous, and it means that it is a book for recording the deeds of the heroes of the children of Israel. It is a historical book and not one of the books of the Holy Bible, and in it were written the accounts of Joshua's victory over the five kings (Josh 10:13), and they are an abbreviation of the name Jeshurun, that is, beloved Israel.

1.15.3.en: David commanded that the children of Judah learn this song, which was called "the song of the bow," because the bow was one of the weapons of war in that time and signifies valor and skill in those wars, which are the qualities the song highlighted. And because Jonathan excelled in the use of the bow and arrows, and David loved Jonathan very much, he called the lament the song of the bow. The purpose of preserving the song was to perpetuate the memory of Saul, Jonathan and the brave warriors. The song was taught first to the children of Judah as the tribe of David, and afterwards all the tribes learned it.

1.16.0.en: The roe: the male gazelle, which leads the herd and is distinguished by courage and leadership.

1.16.2.en: David likens both Jonathan and Saul to the gazelle for their swiftness of movement and courage in fighting, and he mourns them because they were killed on Mount Gilboa, the lofty mountain, just as they themselves were great and lofty in their lives. David marvels at the fall of the heroes of Israel in this war, they who had always been victorious in all the previous wars.

1.17.0.en: In his poem David calls on them not to spread the news of Israel's defeat in the cities of the Philistines such as Gath and Ashkelon, nor in their streets, where people gather in crowds and news travels quickly, lest the women and daughters of the Philistines rejoice and gloat over the death of Saul and his soldiers. He called them "daughters of the uncircumcised" because they are a people foreign to the Lord who did not enter into a covenant with Him by circumcision. He chose Gath because it is the largest of the Philistine cities, and he chose Ashkelon because it has the largest temples of the goddess Ashtaroth. Perhaps the Philistines had sent the weapons of Saul and Jonathan to the temples of Ashkelon to show the power of their gods, who had won the victory in the war (1 Sam 31:10).

1.18.0.en: The shield: the large shield, a piece of wood covered with leather to ward off arrows from the warrior's body.

1.18.1.en: The mountains of Gilboa were the places where the soldiers and heroes of Israel fell, so David called down drought upon them, that neither rain nor dew would water them, and that no crops would grow in them from which tithes and offerings might be presented, so that the blessing would be removed from them. David explains the reason for his curse upon the place, because Saul, Jonathan and the rest of the heroes died there, and their weapons were cast down upon it, among them the large shield belonging to King Saul, which was anointed with the holy oil (as commanders were accustomed to do with their weapons in order to receive a blessing), and this holy anointing was lost through its being cast upon the ground, and every trace of the holy oil was gone.

1.19.0.en: In all their previous victories David remembers the valor and boldness of Saul and Jonathan, and their weapons that shed the blood of the enemies and brought down the bodies of their mighty soldiers. In all those wars Jonathan never turned back as cowards do, and his sword reaped the heads of the enemies in all the rounds of battle and never failed in any of them.

1.19.1.en: All the words that David said about Saul were words of praise in which he mentioned his good qualities and did not mention his wrongdoings. If someone sins against us, may we remember his virtues and not the mistakes he fell into.

1.20.0.en: The people loved and were attached to the leadership and kingship of Saul and of his son, the crown prince Jonathan, and the two of them also loved their people and worked to fulfill its hopes.

1.20.1.en: Saul and Jonathan lived clinging to one another and were not separated, neither in peace nor in war. As they were side by side in their lives, so they were also in their deaths. Both were lighter and swifter in movement than eagles, and stronger than lions in strength and courage in wars.

1.21.0.en: Scarlet: a dark red color, and scarlet clothes were the clothes of kings and the rich. David calls on the women of Israel to weep for Saul, whose reign was a reign of prosperity and ease, in which the women enjoyed the finest clothes, the beautiful royal red clothes, and wore ornaments of gold.

1.22.0.en: He returns and marvels at the death of the mighty men Saul and Jonathan, and especially his friend Jonathan, who died on the mountains of Gilboa.

1.23.0.en: David shows his deep grief over the death of his friend, whom he considered closer to him than a brother, so that his death was like a great shock that shook him to the depths. Jonathan's dealings with David had been exceedingly gentle and sweet, and David returned to him feelings of affection and love, so that their friendship became a proverb. Indeed, their love for one another was stronger and more wonderful than the love of a woman for a man, for it was free of every ulterior motive, an innocent and self-sacrificing love, each preferring the other to himself. Jonathan had served David by rescuing him from his father Saul, and David wanted to repay Jonathan's kindness when he became king, but sadly Jonathan died in the war with Saul, and David had no opportunity to express his love for Jonathan except by this lament, though David also tried to honor Jonathan's sons, such as Mephibosheth (ch. 9).

1.24.0.en: David returns once more and repeats his marvel at the death of the mighty men Saul and Jonathan, and asks in astonishment how the weapons lost their effectiveness in the war, so that their effect vanished as if they had melted away. Thus we find David mentioning Saul's virtues and forgetting his sins, because David is characterized by a simple outlook and by love even toward those who are hostile to him.

1.24.1.en: The clash between Abner and Joab

2.0.s.en: (1) David's reign over Judah and his blessing of Jabesh Gilead

2.0.0.en: Hebron: a city in the land of Judah built on the mountains and easy to defend. It was originally called "Kirjath-arba," and Hebron had villages dependent on it, and it was one of the cities of refuge. It is one of the oldest cities in the world and lies 30 km south-west of Jerusalem. It is now the city of Hebron (al-Khalil), and in it is the cave of Machpelah, in which Abraham, Isaac and Jacob and their families were buried.

2.0.1.en: With the death of Saul, David found that there was no point in his remaining in Ziklag and that it was better for him to return to his homeland and his people. But as was his custom, he took no decision except after inquiring of the Lord, so he asked Him whether he should go up to one of the cities of Judah, and the Lord answered him yes. Then he asked to which city he should go, and the Lord answered him that he should go to Hebron. We see here David seeking God before everything, in peace as in war, because he had become accustomed to seek Him always.

2.0.2.en: Take care to seek God's counsel before any work, and God will answer you in different ways, such as through your father of confession, or through the Holy Bible, or in any other way. Whatever you desire in the matter, make sure through prayer that God agrees to it.

2.1.0.en: David went up to Hebron with his two wives Ahinoam and Abigail, who had been the widow of Nabal the Carmelite. As for his wife Michal, the daughter of Saul, she was still with Phalti, to whom Saul had given her (1 Sam 25:44).

2.2.0.en: David cared for his companions who had accompanied him during Saul's pursuit of him, so he brought them and their households to Hebron and the cities and villages dependent on it.

2.3.0.en: Jabesh Gilead: a city on Mount Gilead east of the Jordan, now called "Wadi Yabis." It seems that they had a strong relationship with the tribe of Benjamin, from which King Saul came, for they did not join the tribes of Israel in fighting against this tribe when it sinned in the matter of the Levite's concubine (Judg 20, 21), and now they care for Saul's body, and Saul may have cared for them during his reign.

2.3.1.en: The elders of the tribe of Judah gathered to David in Hebron as representatives of the tribe and proclaimed him king over their tribe. These elders knew that David had already been anointed by Samuel during Saul's lifetime, so it was natural that he be installed officially after the death of Saul.

2.3.2.en: The men of Judah told David of what the people of Jabesh Gilead had done, an action that showed courage and loyalty, for they risked their lives and went to where the bodies of Saul and his sons were and took them down from the wall of Beth-shan, where the Philistines had hung them to disgrace them (1 Sam 31:10-12), and carried them to their city, where they buried them.

2.3.3.en: Thus David was anointed king in three stages:

2.3.4.en: 1- He was anointed king secretly in the house of his father Jesse by the hand of Samuel (1 Sam 16:13).

2.3.5.en: 2- He was anointed king over the tribe of Judah in this verse.

2.3.6.en: 3- He was anointed king over all the tribes of the children of Israel (ch. 5:3). In this he is a type of Christ, who was anointed king three times:

2.3.8.en: 2- On the Cross, by paying the debt that was upon us, He reigned over everyone who believes in Him and saved them from the hand of the devil.

2.3.9.en: 3- In the Kingdom of Heaven, when He reigns forever over the hearts of those who believe in Him.

2.4.0.en: David sent a blessing and prayer for good to the people of Jabesh Gilead for what they had done with the bodies of Saul and his sons, and promised that he too would repay them for their kindness.

2.4.1.en: How beautiful that David began his reign by blessing and encouraging his people and not by blame or punishment. When a person begins his work or his meetings, it must be with gentleness and encouragement. Likewise, he made use of the enthusiasm of the people of Jabesh Gilead, who loved Saul the former king, and he did not reject them because Saul had been his enemy, but with wisdom he tried to win them in order to use their enthusiasm and energy in his new kingdom. It is good for a person to make use of all the energies around him, and with love to encourage everyone and win all.

2.5.0.en: David comforts them over the death of Saul and asks them to be strong like mighty men, and tells them that he has become king over the tribe of Judah, and perhaps by this he is inviting them to submit to him.

2.6.0.en: Ishbosheth: the fourth son of Saul, who did not die in the war with the Philistines, while his other three brothers died. He is Eshbaal mentioned in (1 Chr 8:33), and the name was changed to Ishbosheth because of their hatred of the name Baal, which is a pagan god.

2.6.1.en: Mahanaim: the meaning of its name is two camps, and it lies east of the Jordan and north of the River Jabbok. There Jacob saw the host of angels and called it Mahanaim, referring to two camps, that is, his wives and children and the host of angels. It lies on the border of the territory of Gad and Manasseh and is divided into two parts, one belonging to Gad and the other to Manasseh, and Gad's part was given to the children of Merari, so it became a city of refuge (Josh 21:38). Abner was seeking to keep his position as commander of the army, so when Saul was killed in the war he took Ishbosheth and came to the city of Mahanaim on the east bank of the Jordan, where he proclaimed him king over the rest of the tribes of Israel, and he took that town as the capital of the kingdom. Abner knew the weakness of Ishbosheth's character, as shown by Ishbosheth's not taking part with his father in the battle against the Philistines, or perhaps he fled from the battle, and so Abner would become the real head of the kingdom, especially as he was a relative of King Saul, being his cousin (1 Sam 14:50). Thus Abner began to be hostile to David after he became king, and he wanted to seize Judah also, as shown by his fighting against it several times throughout the seven years in which David reigned in Hebron.

2.7.0.en: Gilead: a city in the plains of Gilead east of the Jordan.

2.7.1.en: The Ashurites: what is meant is the tribe of Asher (the Asherites). Jezreel: a city in the mountains of Judah.

2.7.2.en: The kingdom of Ishbosheth included several regions, among them Gilead, the lands of Jezreel, the tribe of Asher, the tribe of Ephraim and the tribe of Benjamin, in addition to the rest of the tribes except the tribe of Judah.

2.8.0.en: Ishbosheth was forty years old when he was proclaimed king over Israel, and he remained in his reign only two years, then he was killed by his servants as will come in (ch. 4), and the tribe of Judah did not submit to him, but remained steadfast in following David.

2.8.1.en: Ishbosheth was 35 years old at the death of Saul his father, and David remained king five years in Hebron, then Abner brought about this division when Ishbosheth reigned in Mahanaim. This division lasted only two years, so the kingdom is considered to extend through the days of Saul, David and Solomon, and the division took place after the death of Solomon.

2.9.0.en: The capital of the kingdom of Judah, which was subject to David, was Hebron, where David reigned seven years and six months. (David's reign lasted forty years, of which seven years and six months were in Hebron and thirty-three years in Jerusalem.)

2.9.1.en: Do not care for your own interest at the expense of those around you, setting up divisions and problems and disturbing others, for you will lose your own peace too, and it is the most important thing. Rather, seek peace with others as much as you can, and win those around you with love, so that you keep your peace even if the hearts of those around you have evil in them, because you are seeking the good.

2.10.0.en: Gibeon: a city about 8 km north of Jerusalem. The Gibeonites are the ones who deceived Joshua long ago and joined the children of Israel (Josh 10:6). After Abner made Ishbosheth king over all the tribes except Judah, he coveted taking Judah, so he declared war between himself and David's army, which was led by Joab, and they met at a pool beside Gibeon.

2.11.1.en: Abner called for a bloody duel between two groups of soldiers from the two armies, so that if one group won over the other, the king of the winning group would be king over all Israel, or perhaps he wanted to test the strength of the soldiers of Joab's army. (This event reminds us of what Goliath the Philistine proposed at the confrontation between the army of the Philistines and the army of Israel under Saul (1 Sam 17:8-11).)

2.12.0.en: Abner noticed the weakness of the two sides' inclination to fight, so he proposed choosing a team of twelve men from each side to carry out the duel, a team of the men of the tribe of Benjamin, subject to Ishbosheth, for Saul was of the tribe of Benjamin, and the other team of David's men, picked out from among the two armies in preparation for the confrontation.

2.13.0.en: Helkath-hazzurim: the field of swords, where the swords reaped the lives of the soldiers.

2.13.1.en: The commanders' proposal for the confrontation mentioned was a mad proposal with which the duelists of both sides were not convinced, so the encounter between them did not last long, for they agreed among themselves that each combatant would seize the head of the other and strike his fellow in his side, killing him quickly so that he would die without prolonged torment. That is, they did not duel, but each group killed the other, and the encounter in this form was a tragedy, so the place where its events took place was called "the field of the sword." Here we see the hardness of heart of Abner and Joab, who are like the Romans who loved the shedding of blood and made light of the lives of their followers. The soldiers of both sides felt that their lives had no value, so they agreed that each group would kill the other.

2.14.0.en: The duel produced no solution, for the twenty-four fighters of both sides fell without any display of fighting skill by either side to show the superiority of one side over the other. When the two armies saw that the matter had not been decided in this way, a fierce battle took place between them, which ended in the defeat of Abner's army before David's men.

2.15.0.en: Joab, Abishai and Asahel: the three commanders of David, who are the sons of "Zeruiah," David's sister on his mother's side.

2.15.1.en: "As a wild roe": the male gazelle that runs swiftly in the wilderness.

2.15.2.en: The inspired text tells us here of another tragedy that took place between Asahel, the brother of both Joab and Abishai, and Abner, the commander of Ishbosheth's army. The three brothers were leading David's companies, and Asahel was swift of foot like a gazelle, so he ran after Abner, turning neither to the right nor to the left, in order to overtake him and kill him. This was without consulting his two brothers, that is, it was a rash impulse on his part to deliver Judah and David from Abner.

2.15.3.en: Recklessness and rashness lead to needless pitfalls, for sometimes ambition that is not well considered brings misery and wretchedness to the one who rushes toward it without wisdom. Good intentions alone are not enough unless they are accompanied by wisdom and sound planning.

2.16.0.en: Abner looked behind him and saw the one who was following him in order to overtake him, and knew that it was Asahel, so he asked him in disapproval, "Art thou Asahel?" (The disapproval here is because he saw that Asahel by this deed was being rash and that this pride of his would not be to his benefit.)

2.17.1.en: Abner advised him to look for a warrior who would be his equal in experience, so that he might fight with him and take spoil from him, and not expose himself to the danger of a duel with a trained commander, who was Abner himself, but Asahel refused the advice and continued his pursuit of Abner.

2.18.0.en: "Smite thee to the ground": kill you.

2.18.1.en: "How then should I hold up my face": I will be in a critical position in which I cannot defend my stand.

2.18.2.en: Abner repeated his advice to Asahel, asking him to stop pursuing him, or else he would face him and kill him in self-defense against his recklessness. He also made him understand that if he killed him, he would be blamed by his elder brother Joab and would not be able to justify his act before him. He was not afraid of Asahel, but he feared that he would kill him and a clash would occur between him and Joab.

2.19.0.en: The hinder end of the spear: the rear of the spear, the end of the shaft of the spear.

2.19.1.en: Asahel did not want to accept the advice and turn back, so Abner was compelled, in defense of himself, to face him and strike him in the belly until the shaft of the spear came out behind him, and he died on the spot. Everyone who passed the place where Asahel fell stood still, remembering this painful event of a brave young man in the prime of his life, dear to his brothers and to everyone. But Asahel erred in that he relied on his swiftness in running and did not rely on God, forgetting Abner's skill in war, so God allowed Abner to kill him.

2.20.0.en: Joab and Abishai sought to pursue Abner to avenge their brother Asahel, whom Abner had killed, and the pursuit continued until sunset, and in their pursuit they had come to a hill near one of the villages of Benjamin on the way of the wilderness surrounding Gibeon, which is called the hill of Ammah.

2.21.0.en: Abner's aim in reaching one of the villages of Benjamin was that the men of the children of Benjamin might join him to strengthen his army and reorganize its ranks. This is in fact what happened, for the men of Benjamin were eager to join him, defending out of their feelings Ishbosheth the king, who was of their own tribe.

2.22.0.en: "The latter end": the end of the civil war, if it continues.

2.22.1.en: Abner warned Joab that if the war continued it would become a civil war in which many of the children of Israel would die, and he invited him to make peace. Abner did not call for the halting of the war except when a great number of his army had been killed and he himself was exposed to death, though he was the one who had begun it and made light of the lives of the soldiers whom he had asked to duel. So he is selfish, thinking of himself, and he made light of the lives of others.

2.23.0.en: Joab swore to him that he was certain that the cause of this ill-fated war was his proposal, made in the morning of that same day, that two teams from the two sides should duel, for if he had not done that, the soldiers of both parties would have gone their own way and those futile battles would not have occurred. By this he held him responsible for this war.

2.24.0.en: Joab responded to Abner's call despite his having laid the blame for the war on him, and blew the trumpets as a signal to the men to stop the fighting, so his men stopped pursuing the soldiers of the tribes of Israel, and the war between the two sides ended.

2.24.1.en: May you seek peace, and if a quarrel or enmity occurs with someone, take care to remove it in order to keep your peace and the peace of others. This is not weakness, but strength, to seek after peace.

2.25.0.en: After the fighting, which took place west of the Jordan, stopped, Abner and his men marched all night in the desert lands west of the Jordan, then crossed the Jordan to its east bank and walked in the mountain passes until they reached the capital of Ishbosheth's kingdom, which is "Mahanaim."

2.26.0.en: Joab also stopped pursuing Abner and his men, and a count was made of the two sides, and it was found that the number of dead from Joab's army was nineteen soldiers in addition to Asahel, while the loss in the men of Abner's army was much heavier, reaching three hundred and sixty dead. Joab agreed to stop the war because he knew David's desire to stop the civil war, and that he did not want to obtain the kingdom by fighting Ishbosheth and Abner, and also because David had promised Saul that he would preserve his descendants.

2.27.0.en: Joab's soldiers carried the body of their brother Asahel and buried him in his father's tomb in Bethlehem, then continued their march all night until they reached Hebron, the residence of their king David, the next morning. Abner pledges allegiance to David as king
